papers.title: From Depth to Safe Depth: Uncertainty-Aware Monocular Perception for Mobile Robot Navigation
papers.authors: Saeid Firouzi Daghigh, Saeed Ayat
papers.abstract: Monocular depth foundation models make it tempting to replace depth sensors on mobile robots with a single RGB camera. We show that, used off the shelf, this is unsafe: in a simulated indoor navigation benchmark, a standard Nav2 stack driven by Depth Anything V2 (metric) collides in 63\% of 120 episodes, because the model systematically over-estimates the distance to nearby obstacles. We propose a lightweight plug-in module that turns predicted depth into \emph{safe depth}. A 0.58\,M-parameter head on top of the \emph{frozen} depth model predicts, per pixel, a log-depth correction $μ$ and an uncertainty $σ$, trained with a $β$-weighted Gaussian negative log-likelihood. The navigation stack consumes the one-sided bound $\hat d_{\text{safe}}=d\,e^{μ-kσ}$, where $k$ is set by conformal calibration on a held-out world, and uncertainty also decides which pixels may be treated as floor. The correction halves the depth error (AbsRel $0.262\rightarrow0.134$) and reduces near-range over-estimation from 59.8\% to 12.0\%. In navigation, safe depth raises the success rate from 37\% to 70\% and lowers collisions from 63\% to 3\%, close to the 2\% of ground-truth depth. A constant safety margin calibrated to the same pixel coverage reaches only 30\% success because it freezes the robot; uncertainty-aware safety wins 52 of 56 discordant paired episodes against it. Gains hold on glass, texture-less walls and dark regions.

papers.title: FlashMotion: Ultra-Fast Long-Term 3D Motion Generation
papers.authors: Kaixing Yang, Xulong Tang, Ronghui Li, Xiangyue Zhang, Ziqiao Peng, Mingshuang Luo, Chenxi Zhao, Haoyu Wu, et al.
papers.abstract: 3D human motion generation plays a crucial role in game development, extended reality (XR), digital humans, and embodied simulation. Beyond motion generation, practical pipelines include rigging, retargeting, and rendering, making ultra-fast long-term 3D motion generation without compromising quality valuable for real-time interactive applications. Despite promising progress, high-quality long-horizon motion generation under tight inference budgets remains challenging, owing to 2 coupled bottlenecks: (1) generative strategies that require many sampling steps for high-quality 3D motion generation and (2) model architectures with substantial per-step computational and memory costs for long sequences. We present FlashMotion, a co-designed framework for high-quality long-horizon 3D motion generation under a strict inference budget, covering text-to-motion, music-to-dance, and speech-to-gesture tasks. To enhance trajectory-level efficiency, we introduce a 3D motion-space MeanFlow formulation with kinematic and dynamic consistency constraints for few-step generation, together with an Adaptive Soft masking mechanism for temporally coherent motion editing. To improve per-step efficiency, we design a lightweight non-autoregressive BiMamba architecture with condition-guided state selection and AdaIN-based condition fusion mechanism, enhancing cross-modal alignment and generalization to longer motion sequences. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FlashMotion achieves overall state-of-the-art performance in both quality and efficiency across text-to-motion, speech-to-gesture, and music-to-dance generation. Code is available at FlashMotion (https://github.com/Sun-Happy-YKX/FlashMotion).

papers.title: Few-Shot Residual Adaptation of Pretrained Latent World Models
papers.authors: Jakub Suliga, Pankhuri Vanjani, Nisarga Nilavadi, Wolfram Burgard, Rudolf Lioutikov
papers.abstract: Pretrained latent world models can support visual planning and control, but their predictions may fail when physical dynamics change at deployment. We study whether such models can adapt from only a few interactions without modifying their pretrained weights or identifying the changed physical parameters. We introduce a few-shot residual adaptation approach that learns self-supervised corrections from latent prediction errors. The corrections are applied both inside the latent predictor and directly to its predicted latent state, while the pretrained world model remains frozen. We evaluate the approach in simulation and on a real robot under center-of-mass and friction shifts. These changes reduce the success of the frozen model to near zero. Using three interaction episodes for adaptation, our dual-site approach recovers 90\% success under the center-of-mass shift and 100\% under the modified friction on the real robot. Ablations show that correcting both locations outperforms single-site adaptation. Our diagnostics further suggest that much of the learned correction reduces a general prediction mismatch, while successful control also depends on shift-specific information captured during adaptation.

papers.title: Faster but Not Different: Parity-Checked Deployment of the SmolVLA Robot Policy on a Jetson Xavier NX
papers.authors: Nodirov Jakhongir
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies are now small enough for embedded GPUs, but compiling one for such hardware can change its actions without raising any error. We deploy SmolVLA, a 450M-parameter VLA policy, on an NVIDIA Jetson Xavier NX and make agreement with the reference implementation a precondition for every speed-up. The policy is exported as three static ONNX graphs (the vision encoder, the VLM prefix and one step of the action expert), its flow-matching loop runs in a C++17 runtime, and every split point is compared with LeRobot's own fp32 tensors, frozen from real LIBERO frames. With TensorRT 8.5, fp32 engines match LeRobot to 1.6×10−5 action standard deviations at 1.0 s per 50-action chunk. fp16 engines run 3.1 times faster, at 0.33 s, and stay within 0.060 standard deviations, inside the range of the bf16 precision LeRobot itself runs this checkpoint in. They do so only once every layer the graph types as fp32 is pinned to fp32: TensorRT 8.5's default fp16 build returns finite actions unrelated to the reference. We describe this and four further pitfalls the parity checks exposed, and release the code, measurements and figures.

papers.title: FAME-QP: A GPU-Accelerated Quadratic-Programming Solver for Real-Time Model Predictive Control
papers.authors: Santosh Mohan Rajkumar, Debdipta Goswami, Stephanie Stockar
papers.abstract: We present FAME-QP, a GPU-accelerated solver for dense quadratic programs arising in linear model predictive control. FAME-QP combines constraint-dependent operator representations with fused single- and two-kernel iterations replayed through CUDA graphs, automatically selecting the execution configuration through device calibration and problem-specific timing. It probes a cached operator bank to select the initial penalty and updates operators lazily when problem matrices change. Numerical benchmarks and simulated humanoid and quadrotor control experiments demonstrate reduced latency relative to competing GPU solvers while maintaining solution accuracy and control performance.

papers.title: ExRL: Sample-Efficient Online Adaptation of Long-Chunk Policies via Execution Length Control
papers.authors: Xu Luo, Jiaying Yang, Hao Wu, Junlin Xie, Zijin Hong, Ji Zhang, Lianli Gao, Jingkuan Song
papers.abstract: Predicting long action chunks, often spanning dozens of timesteps, has become a key ingredient in increasingly capable robot policies. In this paper, we find that adapting these long-chunk policies with existing reinforcement learning (RL) methods can require many online samples due to the high dimensionality of the action chunks being optimized, making such adaptation impractical in real-world scenarios where interaction data are costly to collect. Our key insight is to shift adaptation from optimizing actions to optimizing how long to execute each predicted action chunk. This keeps the adaptation space low-dimensional while its expressivity grows with the chunk size. We thus introduce Execution at the Right Length (ExRL), a simple approach which augments the base policy with a lightweight adapter that predicts the execution length of each chunk and is trained using off-policy RL algorithms. Across simulation benchmarks and real-world robotic tasks, ExRL enables sample-efficient adaptation of a diverse range of long-chunk policies with minimal task-specific hyperparameter tuning.

papers.title: Elastic-WAM: Adaptive Spatiotemporal Imagination for Efficient Robot Control
papers.authors: Haitian Li, Tianfu Li, Xuxi Zhao, Zizheng Liu, Yangcheng Yu, Yiwen Hou, Zeyu Xiao, Mutian Xu, et al.
papers.abstract: World-Action Models improve robot control by predicting future visual dynamics, but iterative video denoising incurs substantial inference overhead. Recent approaches reduce this cost through partial future denoising, yet typically rely on fixed refinement budgets. Our empirical observations reveal that preferred refinement depths vary across tasks and states, while different future regions exhibit varying relevance to action generation. Motivated by these findings, we propose Elastic-WAM, which adaptively allocates world refinement computation across temporal denoising time and spatial future space. A unified spatiotemporal refinement demand field governs when to stop world refinement, how far to advance each denoising step, and which regions to refresh. We parameterize this field with a shared temporal basis and spatial amplitudes, and learn it through a three-stage action-grounded supervised procedure. At inference, the learned field guides recurrent sparse world refinement to improve task success while reducing inference overhead. Evaluations across diverse simulation benchmarks and real-world long-horizon manipulation demonstrate state-of-the-art control performance with reduced inference latency.

papers.title: Ego Guidance: Enhancing Robot Policy Learning with Action-Free Human Egocentric Videos
papers.authors: Lin Long, Tianren Ma, Zhong Chu, Di Wu, Maosong Cao, Qixiang Ye, Junbo Zhao, Shanghang Zhang
papers.abstract: In this paper, we investigate how human egocentric videos can benefit robot policy learning without action supervision. Building on a pretrained VLM, we propose Shared Prediction on Action and Representation (SPAR), an MoT architecture in which future visual state prediction can provide independent and complementary learning signals alongside action prediction. We find that representations learned from egocentric videos improve downstream performance on out-of-distribution robot tasks, with further gains as video data scales. We also study the effects of objective choices and data curation, providing insights into how to leverage action-free videos for scalable robot learning.

papers.title: Early Survivorship and Clinical Outcomes Following Cementless Robotic-Assisted Restricted Kinematic Alignment Total Knee Arthroplasty
papers.authors: Alex M. Hollenberg, Lane H. McCoy, Nicholas M Brown, Andrew M. Schneider
papers.abstract: Background and objective: Kinematic alignment (KA) has gained interest in total knee arthroplasty (TKA) because of its potential to restore native knee anatomy and improve patient outcomes.Robotic-assisted TKA has been adopted to enhance the precision and reproducibility of component positioning.The purpose of this study was to evaluate early survivorship and clinical outcomes following cementless robotic-assisted restricted KA TKA.Methods: A retrospective review was performed of consecutive patients undergoing primary cementless robotic-assisted KA TKA by a single fellowship-trained arthroplasty surgeon between May 2024 and June 2025.Patients with a minimum one-year follow-up were included.A restricted KA philosophy with predefined alignment boundaries was utilized.The primary outcome was survivorship free from aseptic revision.Secondary outcomes included all-cause revision, reoperations, manipulation under anesthesia (MUA), patient-reported outcomes, and radiographic alignment distribution.Results: A total of 100 cementless robotic-assisted KA TKAs were included.Survivorship free from aseptic revision was 100% at a mean follow-up of 22.8±3.2months, with no cases of aseptic loosening.The Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS) physical function increased by 8.0±9.1 points, PROMIS pain interference decreased by 11.5±10.9points, and PROMIS mobility increased by 9.8±8.8 points from baseline.The mean postoperative Forgotten Joint Score (FJS) was 66.0±26.7,and patient satisfaction was 3.6 ± 0.6 on a four-point Likert scale.The MUA was performed in 6% of knees.Postoperative radiographs demonstrated a broad coronal and sagittal alignment distribution consistent with KA principles.Conclusions: Cementless robotic-assisted KA TKA demonstrated excellent early survivorship and favorable patient-reported outcomes at short-term follow-up.Robotic assistance facilitated consistent execution of KA principles while achieving patient-specific alignment targets, supporting the early compatibility of restricted KA with contemporary cementless fixation.

papers.title: DexSeed: Expanding Human Hand-Object Interactions into Robot Demonstrations for Dexterous Policy Learning
papers.authors: Huaijin Pi, Zehong Shen, Yong Wang, Kechun Xu, Changpeng Wang, Dingkun Wei, Xueyang Wang, Wenjia Wang, et al.
papers.abstract: We study how to generate diverse, physically executable robot demonstrations for dexterous vision-language-action (VLA) learning. Existing demonstration-generation methods typically rely on costly teleoperated examples. Meanwhile, human hand--object datasets provide a reusable source, but existing transfer methods mainly reproduce given interactions. Turning these interactions into VLA training data further requires coverage of different objects and manipulation locations, together with executable arm and finger actions, and visual observations. To achieve this, we present DexSeed, a framework for low-cost generation of dexterous robot data from human hand--object interactions. Our key idea is to expand human sequences while preserving their grasps and realizing the resulting motions under arm-tracking dynamics in physics simulation. Specifically, we organize source sequences by grasp mode with shared language descriptions. InteractionMesh-based retargeting and arm trajectory augmentation adapt these sequences to the robot hand, different object geometries, and pick-and-place locations while preserving local hand--object relationships. An RL finger-control policy produces executable rollouts, while the arm tracks precomputed trajectories. Rendered observations and recorded actions from successful rollouts are paired with grasp descriptions to fine-tune a VLA. Experiments show improved contact fidelity in retargeting and more reliable whole-arm execution than the evaluated baselines. Simulation evaluation and real-world deployment further demonstrate that a VLA fine-tuned solely on the generated demonstrations can execute language-specified grasps. Project page: https://robbyant-research.github.io/DexSeed/.

papers.title: DeRep: Learning Depth Representations for End-to-End Navigation in Cluttered Environments
papers.authors: Hanyu Jin, Kenji Shimada
papers.abstract: End-to-end navigation in cluttered environments relies on compact visual representations to support collision avoidance and goal-directed motion. Existing methods typically learn these representations jointly with the policy or through observation reconstruction, which does not explicitly specify what information the representation should preserve. Moreover, they are usually evaluated with a single downstream policy learner, although the benefit of a representation may depend on how the policy is learned. It therefore remains unclear how different representation-learning objectives affect downstream navigation performance and robustness. This work proposes DeRep, a navigation-oriented representation-learning method that combines local bird's-eye-view reachability supervision with depth reconstruction. To compare representation objectives under controlled conditions, we pretrain encoders with a common architecture and freeze them during downstream learning. We evaluate the representations using a linear policy probe, flow-matching imitation learning, and reinforcement learning with PPO. DeRep achieves the lowest linear policy probe prediction error and outperforms reconstruction alone across all six tested PPO conditions. In imitation learning, both reachability-based objectives achieve higher mean success rates than reconstruction alone, with similar mean success rates between the reachability-only and joint objectives. These results demonstrate consistent benefits of incorporating reachability supervision into depth representation pretraining across different downstream learning methods and evaluation conditions. We further deploy the PPO policy with the frozen DeRep encoder in Gazebo and on a physical quadrotor without fine-tuning, demonstrating its capability for zero-shot sim-to-sim and sim-to-real transfer.

papers.title: DDPG-Based Path Planning for Medical Microrobot Vascular Navigation
papers.authors: Mingcheung Wang
papers.abstract: This research focuses on the critical challenge of autonomous path planning for medical microrobots in complex and constrained environments, such as targeted drug delivery and minimally invasive surgery. Traditional planning algorithms often struggle with the dynamic nature and stringent safety requirements of medical applications. To address this, we propose a framework based on deep reinforcement learning (DRL) to train an agent capable of navigating from a start to a target point while adhering to strict safety boundaries. The problem is formulated as a Markov Decision Process (MDP), defining the robot's state by its position and orientation. We systematically investigate and compare two prominent DRL algorithms: Deep Q-Networks (DQN) for discrete action spaces and Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) for continuous control, allowing for finer and smoother movements. A key innovation of this work is the design of a composite reward function tailored for medical scenarios. This function incorporates incentives for reaching the target, penalties for boundary violations and deviations from a predefined safety corridor, and considerations for path efficiency and smoothness. This meticulously crafted reward mechanism ensures that the agent prioritizes safety and precision above all else. The models, built upon Multi-Layer Perceptrons, are trained to optimize the long-term cumulative reward, effectively learning a robust policy for safe and efficient navigation in simulated medical environments. This study demonstrates the significant potential of DRL in developing intelligent and reliable guidance systems for next-generation medical robotics.

papers.title: Camera equalisation of an 11.5x drop in environmental illuminance: four imitation-learning policies on an SO-101 arm
papers.authors: Simon Cowling
papers.abstract: Real-robot benchmarks of learned visuomotor policies often record room illuminance as the lighting condition. We show that, on a typical low-cost rig, room light and image light can be almost unrelated. Four imitation-learning policies (ACT, SmolVLA, Diffusion Policy and pi0.5) were trained on the same 50 demonstrations of a pick-and-place task on an SO-101 arm. Each was run for ten rollouts at about 520 lux and again at about 45 lux, an 11.5x reduction. Success was 20/40 in normal light and 19/40 in low light: a change of -2.5 percentage points (95% CI -23 to +19), with no evidence that the policies differed in sensitivity (interaction p = 0.86). The recorded video shows why: mean image brightness was only 3% lower in low light on the front camera and 19% lower on the wrist camera. Both cameras were set to automatic exposure and white balance, which most likely absorbed the difference; exposure was not locked in this experiment. An accidental repeat of one 10-rollout block reproduced its success count (7/10) but matched the first block at only 6 of 10 placements, consistent with chance. We conclude that lux alone does not describe what a policy sees. Camera settings, and image statistics compared with the training recordings, are the quantities to report and control. Data and code are public.

papers.title: CIALLO: Learning Shared Intent Representations for Cross-Embodiment Manipulation
papers.authors: Choo Sin Wai, Dake Zhong, Jingye Zhang, Zhifang Liu, Siyao Xiao, Zirong Ding, Yuhong Zhang, Kangjie Chen, et al.
papers.abstract: Robot demonstrations contain reusable manipulation knowledge, but transferring this knowledge across embodiments requires representations that bridge differences in control interfaces. Action reconstruction alone does not ensure that similar behaviors across robots share a representation. To address this gap, we introduce CIALLO, an action codec that aligns actions, visual changes, and observation-grounded language in a shared space of short-horizon behavioral intent. An embodiment-conditioned decoder maps this intent back to robot-specific actions, allowing a shared representation to support different control interfaces. After pretraining on eight embodiments, CIALLO adapts to a new robot from one recording of at most 10 seconds by updating only its embodiment embeddings. The calibrated codec then remains frozen while a policy learns to predict intent from observations and instructions. We instantiate this policy with Qwen3.5-4B to form Qwen-CIALLO, whose backbone requires no large-scale robot-action pretraining before policy finetuning. With 20 demonstrations per task, Qwen-CIALLO achieves 76.7\% average success across real SO-101 and single-arm Piper robots, compared with 70.0\% for fully finetuned $π_0$. In simulation, we additionally finetune the action decoder, achieving 97.3\% success on LIBERO and 52.7\% on RoboTwin 2.0. The LIBERO policy also achieves 80.8\% on LIBERO-Plus without further finetuning. Together, these results support a shared action codec as a transferable control interface that separates embodiment calibration from task learning.

papers.title: Building a robotic self
papers.authors: Martin V. Butz, Verena V. Hafner, Pablo Lanillos
papers.abstract: Abstract I wake up in the morning, I see my hand and I know it is me. This seemingly simple skill lies at the foundation of our agentive selves. We assume that the development of the self, in both biological and synthetic agents, is grounded in sensorimotor embodiment and inductive learning biases, as well as in the principle of predictive coding. Here, we explore the core inductive biases and process components for building a robotic minimal self. We propose that the formation of a hierarchical, generative model of the self is driven by active inference processes that interactively infer both an endogenous contextual frame and behaviour within this frame. Accordingly, experimental implementations in humanoid robots show how body ownership and agency can develop as foundational computational components. This work on building a robotic minimal self outlines future research directions in mechanistic modelling of the development of an artificial self. To probe the depth of this development, we sketch out embodied Turing tests that challenge complex problem-solving skills, as well as social intelligence and theory of mind. We suggest that uncertainty resolution and the social domain may be promising avenues for further research in the near future. This article is part of the discussion meeting issue ‘From being to identity: analysis and synthesis of the self’.

papers.title: BODYinTRANSIT-Lab: A Multimodal Dataset for Investigating Sensory-Driven Transformations in Body Perception and Affective Experiences
papers.authors: Mohammad Mahdi Dehshibi, Tomás Martínez Cortés, Amar D'Adamo, Daniel de la Prida, Luis-Antonio Azpicueta-Ruíz, Laia Turmo Vidal, Marte Roel Lesur, Joaquín R. Díaz-Durán, et al.
papers.abstract: Multimodal datasets that combine synchronised behavioural and physiological signals with subjective affective and body perception measures are still rare. This limits both the understanding of embodied experience and the development of computational models that infer subjective states from sensor data. We introduce BODYinTRANSIT-Lab, a multimodal dataset that addresses this gap by capturing affective, perceptual, and behavioural responses to the Footsteps Illusion. In this closed-loop paradigm, participants perform walking tasks while receiving real-time manipulated auditory feedback of their own footsteps intended to alter perceived body weight. The dataset comprises synchronised recordings from 101 participants recruited through systematic stratification by eating-disorder symptomatology and physical activity level. BODYinTRANSIT-Lab combines full-body kinematics with electromyography, electrocardiography, respiration, and electrodermal activity. Its annotations capture both immediate and post-trial experience, including within-trial perceived-weight ratings, post-trial assessments of body feelings and affective experience, 3D avatar body visualisations, and quantitative body maps. Psychological, behavioural, demographic, and social measures provide further information about factors that may influence individual responses. We provide a deep learning benchmark that uses walking kinematics to classify relative affective valence and perceived weight within subjects. On within-session, segment-level splits, the baseline model achieved mean balanced accuracies of 45.9% for affective valence and 44.5% for perceived weight. The BODYinTRANSIT-Lab dataset provides an experimentally controlled resource for cognitive neuroscience and affective computing research, with potential applications in affect-aware interactive systems, health and well-being technologies, and creative embodied experiences.

papers.title: An Iontronic Bimodal Afferent Nerve for Cross‐Modal Neuromorphic Fusion and Robotic Sorting
papers.authors: Mengkang Deng, Wenxin Cao, Xinci Gong, Jiangdong Gong, Hang Xu, Wenjing Wang, Chentao Du, Wang Meng-Fei
papers.abstract: Inspired by the multisensory perception and fusion strategy of the biological tactile system, we present a bimodal iontronic afferent nerve that integrates a flexible pressure-temperature sensor patch, pulse-encoding electronics, an electrolyte-gated synaptic transistor and a dual-branch neuromorphic classification framework. The flexible sensor patch enables pressure and temperature perception over broad ranges, covering mechanical stimuli from 0 to 300 kPa and thermal stimuli from 0°C to 80°C. Rather than functioning as an isolated sensor, the system converts mechanical and thermal tactile cues into unified iontronic/spiking representations, enabling neuromorphic encoding, synaptic modulation and cross-modal feature fusion. By integrating pressure and temperature features through a dual-branch neuromorphic network, the system achieves 92.00% accuracy under within-recording contiguous-block validation with dual-feature fusion and outperforming single-modal classification. Finally, the integrated afferent nerve is applied to feed-forward robotic tactile sorting, where objects with different color-derived thermal states and mechanical stiffness are identified and classified. This work demonstrates a flexible bimodal neuromorphic tactile system capable of sensing, encoding, fusing and acting on multimodal tactile information, providing a promising route toward artificial skin for intelligent robotic perception.

papers.title: Active Inference and Predictive Processing for Skill Learning: Implications for Skill Acquisition in Coaching Practice
papers.authors: Jon Mackey, Dave J. Collins, Jamie A. Taylor
papers.abstract: This paper explores the potential of the Active Inference Framework (AIF) and Predictive Processing (PP) to advance our understanding of skill and motor learning with a key focus on introducing these concepts to coaches and highlighting their practical implications. Conceptual frameworks such as Information Processing (IP) and Ecological Dynamics (ED) have contributed significantly to the field of skill acquisition. Despite recent efforts to reconcile these perspectives, however, their fundamentally different theoretical foundations concerning perception, cognition and learning processes pose substantial challenges for integration. Although ED has made valuable contributions through its focus on perception-action coupling and direct interaction with the environment, it involves adopting a radical ontological stance that emphasises rejecting traditional cognitive constructs that can complicate practical applications in coaching. Conversely, IP's reliance on concepts such as stored motor programs and the view of the brain as a computer-like processor can limit its ability to account for the dynamic, emergent nature of skill acquisition in real-world contexts. We suggest that AIF offers a parsimonious perspective, accommodating the dynamic, embodied and enactive nature of skill acquisition without the necessity of committing to either framework's specific assumptions. This perspective provides practitioners with a coherent and flexible framework for understanding and designing skill learning interventions, offering a practically useful account of skill acquisition for coaching practice.

papers.title: A human-in-the-loop Control Paradigm for Construction Robotics: From VR-Guided Teleoperation to Semi-Autonomous Dual-Arm Operation
papers.authors: Jinhua Chen, Xiaoji Xu, Zhongyuan Liao, Huang Zhenmin, Zhang Ye, Changying Xiang
papers.abstract: Construction tasks in hazardous and unstructured environments require both human adaptability and robotic precision, yet existing approaches often treat teleoperation and autonomy as separate control modes. This paper presents a human-in-the-loop control paradigm that enables structured transitions among VR-guided teleoperation, semi-autonomous shared control, and rule-based autonomous execution for contact-rich dual-arm construction tasks. The proposed system combines immersive VR guidance, a manually defined library of reusable skill primitives, and a shared-autonomy framework with explicit human-robot role allocation and command-priority rules. This integration allows operators to retain supervisory and corrective authority while delegating repetitive and precision-critical actions to the robot. The paradigm is validated on a dual-arm platform through representative facade-installation tasks. Results show that autonomous execution provides the best performance under well-calibrated nominal conditions, whereas semi-autonomous control improves resilience when environmental disturbances exceed the predefined autonomous pipeline's correction capability. Semi-autonomous control also substantially reduces subjective operator workload compared with full teleoperation. These findings demonstrate that effective construction-robot control should adapt human involvement to task and environmental uncertainty, using autonomy for repeatable operations and shared control for disturbance recovery.

papers.title: A digital twin-based architecture for human-humanoid-machine interaction (DT-H2MI) in smart manufacturing
papers.authors: Mahdi Sadeqi Bajestani, Duhwan Mun, Duck Bong Kim
papers.abstract: Abstract This paper integrates the well-established concepts of digital twins (DTs), human-in-the-loop (HITL) systems, humanoid robots (HRs), and human–machine interaction (HMI) to introduce a conceptual architecture for smart manufacturing. DT-H 2 MI offers a transformative approach to enhancing interactions between humans, humanoids, and machines by creating an advanced digital replica of a physical system that not only mirrors and simulates real-world assets but also incorporates artificial intelligence and cognitive capabilities. Leveraging real-time data streams and cloud/edge computing platforms, DT-H 2 MI is designed to enable dynamic interactions, thereby improving manufacturing efficiency and flexibility. This framework aligns with Industry 5.0’s principles, aiming to enhance sustainability, resiliency, and human-centrism within manufacturing operations. By introducing humanoids into a unified DT framework, the architecture is intended to support seamless human–machine interaction and cognitive automation, with the aim of achieving real-time adaptability beyond conventional Industry 4.0/5.0 approaches. The DT-H 2 MI architecture consists of three fundamental modules: the avatar-human system (AHS), the cyber-physical system (CPS), and the physical artificial intelligence system (PAIS), along with middleware and third-party cloud services. This research lays a crucial foundation for developing the next generation of manufacturing systems and processes, enabling more efficient and intuitive interactions across the manufacturing ecosystem. DT-H 2 MI is presented as a conceptual reference architecture developed following the Design Science Research (DSR) paradigm. A potential welding case study demonstrates how it can be instantiated, rather than providing empirical validation, and its performance claims are formulated as testable propositions with metrics and acceptance criteria for future evaluation.

papers.title: A computational framework for understanding embodied plans
papers.authors: Aalap D. Shah, Basil Saeed, Joshua B. Tenenbaum, Tobias Gerstenberg, Hyowon Gweon, Ilker Yildirim
papers.abstract: Reasoning about people's plans and goals based on their actions is fundamental to human social interaction and essential for cooperative, embodied artificial intelligence. Formalizing this capacity in naturalistic, embodied settings has been a longstanding challenge. Here, we present GenEA, a novel agent representation capable of reasoning over multi-step, long-horizon embodied plans. At the heart of GenEA lies a multilevel state-space that couples the coarse biomechanics of an articulated body and its interactions with nearby objects by extending the task-and-motion planning framework from robotics with simulation-based intuitive physics. By embedding this state-space in a generative model, GenEA yields a joint probability distribution over goals and embodied plans. Across several experiments spanning the qualitatively distinct domains of object manipulation and navigation, featuring diverse tasks and multiple behavioral measures, we show that GenEA, through simple transformations of this joint distribution, recapitulates how humans reason about embodied plans. Crucially, GenEA consistently outperforms strong alternative models, including plausible heuristics, standard task-and-motion planning, and a state-of-the-art vision-language model. GenEA thereby offers a new perspective on the architecture of human reasoning and social cognition, suggesting that embodied artificial intelligence systems seeking to seamlessly interact with humans should adopt GenEA-like generative models of action planning.

papers.title: A Review of Path Planning Methods for Mobile Robots
papers.authors: Liyuan Wang
papers.abstract: Path planning is an indispensable core problem in the autonomous navigation of mobile robots. Whether a safe and efficient trajectory can be planned directly determines the usability of robots in scenarios such as warehousing, delivery, medical assistance and autonomous driving. Scholars at home and abroad have accumulated abundant research results on this problem. Nevertheless, existing methods have respective trade-offs in application scope and performance limits, and no universally recognized optimal solution has been reached so far. This paper sorts out relevant methods. These methods are divided into two categories: traditional methods and intelligent methods. The traditional category includes graph search algorithms (Dijkstra, A*, D*), artificial potential field methods and sampling-based planning algorithms (PRM, RRT, RRT*). The intelligent category covers intelligent optimization methods represented by genetic algorithms, particle swarm optimization and ant colony optimization, as well as two data-driven approaches: reinforcement learning and deep learning. The core idea, typical application scenarios and limitations of each type of method are elaborated one by one. Finally, a horizontal comparison table is provided, and the author puts forward observations on several noteworthy research directions including hybrid planning frameworks, multi-robot coordination and uncertainty modelling.

papers.title: A Meta‐Analysis of the Twin Transition: The Impact of Digitalization on Firms' Eco‐Innovation
papers.authors: Rafael Alberto Iturralde Solórzano, Enrique Acebo, José Ángel Miguel Dávila
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT In the twin transition, firms pursue digitalization and environmental sustainability simultaneously, an effort that draws growing academic interest. However, empirical insights into the relationship between digital technologies and eco‐innovation remain lacking. With a quantitative synthesis and meta‐regression of 38 empirical studies published in high‐impact journals, encompassing 587 effect sizes, the current research clarifies the heterogeneous nature of this relationship across technology types and environmental outcomes. Digitalization is positively and statistically significantly associated with eco‐innovation. Across technology types, artificial intelligence, digital innovation, and smart product platforms show the strongest positive associations, while robotics and Industry 4.0 technologies yield weaker evidence. Across environmental outcomes, the results indicate robust positive associations with green innovation but negative or null associations on average for decarbonization. In revealing that digitalization alone might not be sufficient to achieve emissions reductions without complementary environmental strategies, this study contributes to twin transition literature and clarifies the heterogeneous nature of the digitalization‐eco‐innovation relationships. For managers seeking to balance digital investments with environmental objectives, it also offers practical recommendations.

papers.title: A Cross-Scenario Survey and Analysis of Self-Evolving Multimodal Agents
papers.authors: Jingjing Jiang
papers.abstract: Recent work shows that multimodal agents increasingly self-improve without recurring human annotation. However, each self-improvement mechanism is designed and evaluated within a single scenario, leaving its preconditions unverified under cross-scenario transfer. This survey investigates the structural source of asymmetric mechanism transfer across four scenarios: multimodal reasoning, multimodal generation, GUI and Web navigation, and embodied manipulation. We first formalize the self-evolving multimodal agent by four criteria and a differentia of self-reference, and adopt the three-stage self-evolving loop of experience generation, feedback acquisition, and update consolidation as our analytical framework to position the scenarios along ceilings on rollout count and feedback fidelity. Comparing self-evolving with fixed loops within each scenario separates the limitations that the scenario imposes from those inherent in the self-evolving design. We then recast each mechanism as a trade-off that raises a scarce factor by presupposing a task-structural resource, such as output equivalence or checkable outcomes, and judge it portable, conditional, blocked, or redundant across scenarios. We attribute the asymmetry to divergent combinations of scarce factors and resources across opposite transfer directions, and identify the matched-budget measurements that could overturn these still untested verdicts.

papers.title: A Backdrivable Impedance‐Controlled Wrist for Safe and Measurable Canopy Interaction in Robotic Apple Harvesting
papers.authors: Ali Yasar, Dilshan Ranasinghe, A. M. Atia Ahmed, Andrew, Edric Lay, Shao Liu, Chao Chen
papers.abstract: Unstructured orchard canopies present a major challenge for robotic fruit harvesting, where unpredictable branch contact and visually occluded foliage prevent reliable manipulation using vision alone. Rigid end‐effectors are vulnerable to this interaction, risking damage to gripper and canopy. Just as human pickers rely on physical compliance and tactile feedback to navigate dense canopies, this work presents a compact two‐degree‐of‐freedom backdrivable robotic wrist, the Transparent Robotic Agricultural Wrist (TRAW), designed to accommodate and estimate canopy interaction torques during apple harvesting. A capstan‐driven differential transmission achieves mechanical transparency through passive backdrivability, enabling open‐loop impedance control without passive compliant elements. A dynamic model incorporating gravity compensation enables real‐time sensorless interaction torque estimation from motor current. Benchtop experiments validate the stiffness rendering accuracy (RMS error 0.29 N m rad −1 across 2.00–20.00 N m rad −1 ) and torque tracking performance (RMS error 0.035 N m). Field trials in a commercial apple orchard evaluate wrist compliance during canopy approach and apple envelopment across 120 trials of varying difficulty, demonstrating that the TRAW safely accommodates canopy interaction while characterizing the interaction torques encountered. These results establish wrist‐level compliance with sensorless torque estimation as an effective approach for safe physical interaction in unstructured canopy environments.

papers.title: World In-Context Learning for Agentic Robot Manipulation
papers.authors: Heng Fang, Zehui Guo, Yuehan Zhang, Mingyang Du, Dingkang Liang, Xiang Bai
papers.abstract: Trained action policies write manipulation skill into network weights, tying what is learned to the distribution it is learned from. In-context learning (ICL) avoids this coupling but has not matched trained policies, because a demonstration recorded in another scene carries no feedback from the world the robot currently faces. We observe that what an agent learns in context is semantic, recording task steps and object roles rather than visual appearance, so experience gathered in one world transfers to another. Based on this insight, we propose World In-Context Learning (WICL), a paradigm in which a frozen model starts from a demonstration, rehearses the task in a world such as a simulator, and writes the feedback into its context rather than its weights. We build RoboScript, a modular infrastructure that implements WICL for agentic manipulation. From a single demonstration, RoboScript learns each task through rehearsal in simulation, freezes the learned knowledge as a Task Memory, and deploys the frozen memory on new scenes with data isolation that ensures every deployment input is available on a real robot. On all 50 tasks of RoboTwin 2.0, RoboScript reaches 83.4% mean success across clean and randomized settings with one demonstration per task and no gradient updates, exceeding the strongest trained action policy by over 20 points. The method generalizes across visual distributions, improves through reflection, scales with the foundation model, and transfers to a physical dual-arm robot through cross-embodiment memory adaptation. With a world in the loop, a robot can learn a manipulation task in its context as well as it learns one in its weights. All code is available at https://github.com/ArcheOne-AI/RoboScript

papers.title: WanderBench: Can World Models Explore Dynamic Worlds from Video?
papers.authors: Yuhang Chen, Jiheng Li, Jiale Wang, Zai Wang, Guangyue Liu
papers.abstract: Video world models conditioned on an input video make it possible to explore real, recorded dynamic scenes, enabling re-shooting of footage, free-viewpoint replay, and real-to-sim environments for embodied agents. Such uses require the generated rollout to stay faithful to the recorded world, yet existing benchmarks start from a single image or a text prompt, and video-conditioned generation is evaluated mainly on perceptual quality and camera following. These evaluations do not directly assess whether exploration preserves subject identity, event progression, and scene consistency upon revisiting a location. We introduce WanderBench, a benchmark for exploring dynamic worlds from video. It comprises 745 single-shot source videos of real and AI-generated content in three difficulty tiers (3-25 s), paired with camera routes given as keyboard actions, and evaluates six dimensions with 24 human-validated sub-metrics. Benchmarking eight models, we find that as clips grow longer, models keep the static scene and visual quality but lose camera control and the source dynamics, and that none keeps revisited places consistent. We further propose WanderLand, a training-free framework that conditions each frame of a frozen model on the same-instant source and, on revisits, on its own earlier static content. WanderLand improves five models on every dimension, by up to 8.3 points in source-dynamics fidelity.

papers.title: ViPS: Video-informed Pose Spaces for Auto-Rigged Meshes
papers.authors: Honglin Chen, Karran Pandey, Rundi Wu, Matheus Gadelha, Yannick Hold-Geoffroy, Ayush Tewari, Niloy J. Mitra, Changxi Zheng
papers.abstract: Kinematic rigs provide a structured interface for articulating 3D meshes but lack any associated pose space , i.e., an explicit representation of the plausible manifold of joint configurations for a given mesh. Without such a pose space, stochastic sampling or manual manipulation of raw rig parameters easily results in semantic and/or geometric violations, such as anatomical hyperextension and non-physical self-intersections. We propose Video-informed Pose Spaces (ViPS), a feed-forward framework that discovers the latent distribution of valid articulations for (auto-)rigged meshes by distilling motion priors from a pretrained video diffusion model. Unlike existing methods that rely on scarce, artist-authored 4D datasets, or focus on reconstructing instances of individual motions, ViPS transfers generative video model priors into a universal distribution over the given rig parameterization. Differentiable geometric constraints on the skinned mesh naturally preserve shape-specific geometric consistency without requiring additional (hand-coded) mesh regularization. Our feed-forward model reveals a smooth, compact, and controllable pose space. This, in turn, supports sampling for diverse shape variations, manifold projection for inverse kinematics, and temporally coherent trajectories for animation and keyframing. Further, the distilled 3D pose samples serve as semantic proxies to guide video diffusion, effectively closing the loop between generative 2D priors and structured 3D kinematic control. Our evaluations show that ViPS, trained solely using video priors, matches the performance of state-of-the-art models trained on synthetic artist-created 4D data in both plausibility and diversity. Additionally, as a universal model, ViPS exhibits robust zero-shot generalization to out-of-distribution species and unseen skeletal topologies. Project Page: https://honglin-c.github.io/vips/

papers.title: VLA-MOPD: On-Policy Distillation for Multi-Task VLA Policy Consolidation
papers.authors: Yongxuan Lv, Zhen Fang, Lichen Man, Hao Li, Pu Li, Hengyi Wang, Langfeng Cao, Lin Chen, et al.
papers.abstract: Physical intelligence requires embodied agents to ground language in observations and execute actions while retaining useful skills. Vision-language-action (VLA) policies offer a shared interface, but task-specific post-training often produces separate specialists. Consolidation is difficult: mixed-task reinforcement learning provides sparse trajectory-level credit, while offline distillation may miss student-visited observations and endpoint distillation does not supervise intermediate action-generation states. We introduce VLA Multi-teacher On-Policy Distillation (VLA-MOPD), a protocol for consolidating flow-matching VLA specialists. After acquiring task or suite experts, a shared student collects robot rollouts and queries the instruction-routed frozen teacher at each visited observation and intermediate ordinary differential equation (ODE) state. Detached per-flow-step transition targets supervise valid action chunks through a masked local matching loss; an optional reference-policy term supports retention on other tasks. Starting from one trajectory per LIBERO task, VLA-MOPD raises mean success-once from 75.4% to 98.9%, compared with 98.15% for endpoint action distillation. It improves mean RoboTwin 2.0 success from 73.0% to 89.3%; on a Piper robot, two consolidation rounds improve average success from 70.0% to 90.0%. In a near-matched Spatial-adaptation study, reference matching limits the Object suite decrease to 3.0 points, versus 13.2 without the reference term.

papers.title: VLA Adaptation with Real and Simulated Data: A Case Study on Robotic Chess
papers.authors: Matěj Kripner, Milan Straka
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are trained as general-purpose foundation models for robot learning, and require fine-tuning for each downstream task and robot. This raises practical questions such as how much data and training updates are needed, how checkpoints should be selected, and whether simulation can be leveraged to alleviate the cost of real data collection. We study these questions on a task that requires both precise manipulation and spatial understanding of the scene. In this task, an SO-101 arm moves a chess king between two squares that are given only by their names, such as e4 and a5. We fine-tune $π_{0.5}$ with various dataset sizes and update budgets, using teleoperated demonstrations as well as simulated demonstrations from a randomized scripted expert that imitates the variability of human demonstrations. In simulation, the success rate scales with both data and updates. Importantly, we find that a short learning-rate cool-down adds up to 31 points and is necessary for comparing checkpoints, and that validation loss and action error are unreliable for model selection. On the real arm, we fine-tune on up to 256 teleoperated demonstrations and evaluate ten policies in 25 trials each. Partial results indicate that pretraining on the simulated demonstrations helps substantially, most clearly when real data is scarce. We also present a negative result, in which training on the policy's own rollouts with filtered behavior cloning, RECAP-style advantage conditioning, corrections from an automatic coach, or residual reinforcement learning did not yield a measurable improvement over plain behavior cloning in our setting. We release the simulator, the expert and the real demonstrations.

papers.title: UniffordInteractor: Reasoning the Unified Affordance for Human and Multi-Object Interaction
papers.authors: Chen Su, Xingqun Qi, 胡旭睿, Bingkun Yang, Muyi Sun, Man Zhang, Zhenan Sun
papers.abstract: Deriving plausible and dynamic Human Object Interaction (HOI) has gained tremendous progress in Embodied AI and Immersive AR/VR. While existing HOI methods have effectively explored human interaction with individual or fixed objects, they still show limitations in complex multi-object interaction scenes. Meanwhile, previous approaches focus more on the contact information held by human-object relation, overlooking the significance of the contact situation of various entities ( i.e. , object-object). To address these limitations, we propose UniffordInteractor , a Reasoning-then-Interacting framework that leverages unified affordance for realistic and long-horizon human and multi-object interaction modeling. At the reasoning stage, we devise a Unified Affordance Reasoner (UAR) that employs a fine-tuned 3D Multimodal Large Language Model for unified object-centric affordance prediction. At the interacting stage, we propose Hierarchical Interaction Generator (HIG) , which formulates the interaction generation as a hierarchical ( e.g. , root→body→hand→objects) autoregressive prediction, conditioned on the obtained unified affordance. Extensive experiments demonstrate that UniffordInteractor surpasses SOTA counterparts in human and multi-object interaction generation. Our project page is available at this site. Code and dataset will be released upon publication.

papers.title: UniOMA: Unified Optimal-Transport Multi-Modal Structural Alignment for Robot Perception
papers.authors: Xinrui Zu, Mark Hoogendoorn, Kevin Sebastian Luck, Shujian Yu
papers.abstract: Achieving generalizable and well-aligned multimodal representations remains a core challenge in robot learning. While recent approaches have attempted to align modalities by modeling conditional or higher-order statistical dependencies, they do not explicitly consider the structural coherence across modalities. In this work, we propose a novel multimodal alignment method that augments existing contrastive losses with a geometry-aware Gromov--Wasserstein (GW) distance-based regularization. To this end, we encode intra-modal geometry for each modality and reduce cross-modal structural discrepancies through a dynamically learned GW barycenter, thereby encouraging structural consistency in addition to instance-level contrastive alignment. We apply this optimal-transport-based alignment strategy to robot perception tasks involving underexplored modalities such as force and tactile signals, where modality data often exhibit varying sample densities. Extensive experiments on five robotic benchmarks show that our method improves structural alignment and downstream performance over state-of-the-art multimodal contrastive baselines across a wide range of downstream tasks, including robot and environment state prediction. Moreover, our GW-based regularization can be seamlessly integrated into most InfoNCE-like objectives.

papers.title: TierTac: Physically‐Grounded Hierarchical Reasoning for Generalizable Tactile Perception
papers.authors: Shipeng Lyu, Lijie Sheng, Wenyao Zhang, Chen Yao, Zheng Li, Zhenzhong Jia, David Navarro-Alarcón, Isabel Y.N Guan
papers.abstract: Tactile perception is essential for intelligent robotic systems interacting with the physical world, yet achieving reliable understanding across heterogeneous sensors remains challenging. Existing approaches rely on representation learning or independent attribute prediction, often neglecting the physically grounded hierarchical dependencies underlying contact interactions. Here, we propose TierTac, a physically grounded hierarchical reasoning framework for generalizable tactile perception. TierTac organizes tactile understanding using a physics‐informed dependency hierarchy comprising three levels: intrinsic physical properties, compliance responses, and contact states. It combines contact‐aware, sensor‐agnostic representation learning with hierarchical neuro‐symbolic reasoning to enable physically consistent multiattribute inference. Experiments across multiple datasets demonstrate improved cross‐sensor alignment, physically consistent prediction, and generalization to unseen sensors. Real‐world robotic evaluations further show more stable and physically consistent interactions under both classical control and learned policies. These results highlight physically grounded hierarchical reasoning as an effective principle for developing generalizable tactile intelligence in robotic systems.

papers.title: Thermo-VLA: A Thermal-Aware Vision-Language-Action Model with Gated Residual Modulation for Robotic Manipulation
papers.authors: Jingxuan Chen, Junshi Luo, Chencheng Dong, Xiaojian Nie, Tongge Huang, Qiang Huang
papers.abstract: Recent Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have begun incorporating thermal sensing, but existing approaches typically treat thermal images as ordinary visual inputs, providing limited support for temperature-aware relational reasoning in manipulation. To address this limitation, we propose Thermo-VLA with a ThermoRes Encoder, which decomposes thermal images into cold and hot attribute representations and injects them into the RGB token through language-conditioned residual modulation, enabling temperature-driven target selection and continuous manipulation. We further construct six real-world robotic tasks on a dual-arm Unitree G1 platform, spanning basic grounding to relational reasoning. Experiments show that Thermo-VLA achieves an average success rate of 0.86 across four thermal-dependent tasks, outperforming a pi_0.5 baseline that directly incorporates RGB-thermal observations by 18 percentage points. Under unseen-object and scene variations, Thermo-VLA maintains an average success rate of 0.78, achieving the best generalisation performance among the compared methods. Beyond thermal sensing, we transfer the same residual modulation mechanism to colour attributes and observe consistent improvements in both simulation and real-robot experiments, indicating its potential to generalise beyond thermal attributes. papers.title: The Relative Value of Demonstration Data: Execution Time Limits and Operator Mixtures in Behavior Cloning
papers.authors: Jiaxuan Guo, Xingyu Ren, Youran Sun, Jingxin Yang, Kejia Zhang, Haizhao Yang
papers.abstract: Robot demonstration datasets combine demonstrations from teleoperators of uneven experience, so collection teams need to know how many demonstrations from one group match those from another. We measure this with a data multiple: the ratio of the numbers of demonstrations two groups need for their policies to reach the same success rate. On robomimic's simulated Square and Can tasks, we train behavior-cloning policies on demonstrations from the two teleoperators robomimic labels Better and the two it labels Worse, varying dataset size and the share of Worse demonstrations. On Square, within robomimic's 25-second time limit, an all-Worse training set needs 1.55 times as many demonstrations as an all-Better set. Most of this difference is late completion: policies trained on Worse demonstrations finish later, as the Worse teleoperators do, and with a 100-second limit the multiple falls to 1.11. On Can, most of the difference remains at 100 seconds. If each Worse demonstration were worth 1/1.55 of a Better one, as in an all-Worse set, a half-Better, half-Worse set on Square would need 1.22 times as many demonstrations as an all-Better set. In fact, it needs 13% more than that, and this excess persists at every time limit from 20 to 200 seconds. The excess remains when training draws demonstrations uniformly instead of in proportion to their length. On Square, within the 25-second limit, switching to these Worse teleoperators is cheaper at equal success only if they earn less than a third of the Better teleoperators' hourly pay, because Worse demonstrations also take longer to record.

papers.title: The Algorithmic Gaze
papers.authors: Daniela Oehring
papers.abstract: The integration of AI into clinical medicine is an event in the genealogy of medical visibilities where causal-mechanistic and contextual reasoning are required. Extending Dai and Guo (2025) through Pearl’s causal hierarchy, a four-level taxonomy of consciousness, and a politicized conception of embodied care, this article develops two arguments: (1) only an agent that can be held to account can fail morally, and (2) associative systems cannot take up narrative and contextual material. Five epistemic deficits ground five governance responses, four resting on the knowledge argument; the responsibility argument distinguishes structural conditions from empirical performance and is conditional on non-functionalism.

papers.title: TACTUS: A Robotic Palpation System for Spatially Heterogeneous Hardness Mapping of Woody Breast Myopathy
papers.authors: Chaitanya Pallerla, Yihong Feng, Avisekh Tripathy, Yang Tian, Pouya Sohrabipour, Amirreza Davar, Casey M. Owens, Cengiz Koparan, et al.
papers.abstract: Woody breast (WB) myopathy is a spatially heterogeneous fibro-degenerative condition of the broiler Pectoralis major muscle. Existing mechanical reference methods rely on single-point or sequential compression measurements, limiting characterization of spatial hardness variability. This study presents TACTUS (Tactile Adaptive Conformal 3D Uniform Sensing), an automated tactile array that generates thickness-normalized, three-dimensional hardness maps at 20 anatomically distributed locations within approximately 30 s. TACTUS integrates 20 independently motorized tactuators with force-sensing resistors and encoder-driven linear actuators, alongside a LiDAR depth camera for surface profiling and adaptive compression. The system was evaluated using 100 broiler breast fillets across four WB severity classes (Normal, Mild, Moderate, Severe). TACTUS identified significant force differences among severity classes (ANOVA, p < 0.001), with the strongest differentiation in the cranial region and a significant caudal effect not detected by texture-analyzer measurements. Fillet-level TACTUS force showed moderate but significant correlation with texture-analyzer measurements (Pearson r = 0.441, p < 0.001). Semivariogram, local change entropy, and heterogeneity analyses revealed increasing and anatomically structured hardness variability with WB severity. These findings demonstrate TACTUS as an automated, operator-independent platform for spatially resolved mechanical characterization and ground-truth generation to support hyperspectral and near-infrared spectroscopy-based WB classification systems.

papers.title: Stretchable Electronic Skins Realized by Confined In Situ Silver Patterning on Siloxane‐Modified Polyimide
papers.authors: Jialun Yin, Yongjun Kang, Fangzhou Liu, Yifei Tong, Guofeng Tian, Shengli Qi, Dezhen Wu
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT The rapid development of soft robotics and embodied intelligence demands electronic skins (E‐skins) that are both mechanically self‐adaptive and skin‐conformal. However, the rigid aromatic backbones of conventional polyimides limit stretchability and hinder conformal integration with deformable surfaces. Here, elastically stretchable polyimide (es‐PI) films are developed by incorporating aminopropyl‐terminated siloxane spacers, while a confined‐patterned in situ self‐metallization strategy enables direct fabrication of patterned silver circuits. By spatially confining Ag + coordination and reduction within predefined regions, this strategy produces continuous silver nanolayers with well‐defined boundaries and robust metal–polymer interfaces, preserving electrical integrity during repeated deformation. The selected es‐PI‐0.5 substrate exhibits an estimated nominal elongation at break of approximately 96% and a tensile strength of approximately 25 MPa, while the corresponding metallized film retains electrical continuity during tensile deformation up to 50% strain. Device‐level feasibility is demonstrated through a strain‐dependent inductor–capacitor (LC) resonance response measured using a network analyzer and a separate smartphone‐assisted near‐field excitation experiment with rectified direct‐current (DC) output detected using a multimeter. This work establishes a materials–circuit integration approach for stretchable electronic skins and skin‐mounted sensing demonstrations.

papers.title: Sliding Mode Controller Design for Robotic Manipulator Based on the Hybrid Pigeon‐Inspired Optimization
papers.authors: Xiaohan Liu, Ziwu Ren, Yunxi Miao, Zhongyuan Wang, Yangjun Wang
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT To address the challenge of finding the optimal parameter combination for proportional–integral sliding mode (PISM) controllers in robotic manipulators, this article proposes a novel hybrid pigeon‐inspired optimization (HPIO) algorithm for systematic parameter tuning. The proposed algorithm enhances the conventional PIO framework by incorporating a predation‐inspired random perturbation mechanism and a dynamic population screening strategy, thereby balancing global exploration and local exploitation capabilities. An ablation study validates the individual contributions of the two improvement phases and confirms their synergistic effect on convergence speed and optimization accuracy. Then the HPIO algorithm is employed to optimize the proportional gain , integral gain , and robust gain of the PISM controller, where influences the tracking error response, improves steady‐state accuracy, and enhances robustness to disturbances. Comparative experiments show that HPIO improves the best and mean fitness values relative to PIO and provides a favorable trade‐off between optimization quality and offline computational cost. The proposed method also achieves improved tracking performance under the tested disturbance conditions.

papers.title: Simulating Vein Compressibility for Ultrasound-Guided Femoral Access: Speed, Accuracy, and Phantom Validation
papers.authors: Amit Manicka, Laurent Coulon, Darwin Ang, Michael Loushin, Timothy M. Kowalewski
papers.abstract: In ultrasound-guided femoral access, probe pressure deforms the tissue and changes the vascular anatomy a robot observes. A simulator must reproduce these mechanics fast enough for robotic interaction, yet the computational effort needed for a clinically meaningful signal like vein collapse before artery is unclear. We test the feasibility of a physics-based simulation in NVIDIA's Isaac Sim for Healthcare, with Stable Neo-Hookean tissue solved by Vertex Block Descent on one GPU. A simulation of a low-fidelity cylindrical benchtop phantom with known geometry and mechanical properties, pressed by a robot, predicted its artery within 5 percentage points at every depth. It matched the vein within 3 points through 11 mm of a 25.4 mm press and followed the collapse behavior of the low-fidelity physical phantom. Across element size, time step, and solver iterations, wall clock time per frame scaled linearly with solver work, but accuracy did not improve with more work. The chosen setting reduced solver time per frame by a factor of 976, from 29,700 ms to 30.4 ms, while remaining within 1.03 points of the finest reference setting. The physics solver alone took 30.4 ms per frame, while the full stack, including ultrasound and graphics rendering, took 56.4 ms per frame. Finally, when seeded with realistic literature-based mechanical properties, the digital leg model compressed the vein far more than the artery at every setting, reproducing the expected clinical signal of vein collapse before artery, which is used to distinguish them. In total, these results suggest that the NVIDIA Isaac Sim platform may be suitable for augmenting reinforcement learning training or online simulation for autonomous femoral access with ultrasound.

papers.title: Scale-Consistent Monocular Fisheye Visual Odometry via Spherical Bundle Adjustment-Guided Unsupervised Depth Learning
papers.authors: Wanhui Luo, Hongbo Zhao, Yi Zhou, Qijun Chen, Yiming Nie, Rui Fan
papers.abstract: The wide field of view of fisheye cameras and the simplicity of a monocular setup make monocular fisheye visual odometry (VO) attractive for robotic localization and mapping. Nevertheless, scale drift remains a major challenge over long trajectories. Unsupervised depth learning can help to mitigate this issue, but the pronounced distortion of fisheye images poses challenges for accurate depth estimation. This article presents S$^2$D-FVO, a monocular fisheye VO framework integrating spherical bundle adjustment (SBA)-guided unsupervised depth learning to improve scale consistency and depth estimation accuracy. Given that pixel reprojection residuals do not uniformly reflect angular deviations between viewing rays and that the first-order linearization of a scalar angular reprojection residual is insensitive to perturbations along one tangent direction, SBA employs tangent-space angular reprojection residuals derived from the spherical logarithmic map. These residuals retain sensitivity along both tangent directions, with their norms equal to the corresponding scalar angular residuals. A median depth-based scale regularization term is further integrated into SBA to constrain the reconstruction scale. Building on these formulations, SBA replaces the pose estimation network during unsupervised depth learning, providing more reliable relative poses for view synthesis. In turn, depth estimates from the well-trained depth estimation network provide scale references for SBA, improving scale consistency while allowing individual 3-D landmark positions to be refined. Extensive experiments conducted on multiple public datasets, as well as two newly collected large-scale datasets, demonstrate that the proposed framework outperforms representative existing approaches in both depth and trajectory estimation accuracy and is applicable to different camera models.

papers.title: Safety-Constrained Intelligent Control of a 2-DOF Robotic Manipulator Using Control Barrier Functions
papers.authors: Gabriel da Silva Lima, Made Widhi Surya Atman, Wallace Moreira Bessa
papers.abstract: Control barrier function (CBF) filters depend on dynamic models that can be inaccurate when their parameters and external forces are uncertain. This paper investigates a radial basis function (RBF) neural network compensator whose output is shared by a Cartesian tracking controller and a joint-space CBF filter. An auxiliary state driven by the difference between requested and applied torques corrects the learning signal, reducing the direct influence of filter intervention on adaptation. A two-link manipulator is evaluated through constrained regulation, ablations, matched uncertainty and disturbance trials, and operating-range and timing studies. The results demonstrate that the proposed controller improves tracking while maintaining joint, velocity, and torque limits under parameter uncertainty, and that both the shared compensation and the auxiliary correction contribute to this improvement.

papers.title: SWAM: Scaling World Action Models with Cross-Modal Alignment
papers.authors: Yu Zhou, Xinyuan Xia, Xuankun Yang, Yinghao Yang, Wendi Chen, Bowen Liu, Jianhan Ma, Weicheng Duan, et al.
papers.abstract: World action models jointly predict video and actions conditioned on language. Existing studies focus primarily on architectures and training mechanisms, typically treating language-video alignment acquired through video pretraining as an established foundation. However, introducing action learning may impair this alignment. Principled guidance on data and supervision design for maintaining language-video alignment during action learning remains limited. To investigate this, we curate a pool of approximately 47,000 hours of general videos, egocentric videos, UMI demonstrations, and robot demonstrations. Building on this, we systematically study how language-video supervision, language-video-action supervision, and the joint use of these two forms affect WAM performance. In particular, we examine how language annotation quality affects pretrained language-video capabilities, and how action supervision from UMI and robot demonstrations extends these capabilities to language-video-action modeling. To better scale the model, we further conduct detailed studies on joint training recipe and model architecture. Under a fixed training budget, mixing egocentric videos and UMI demonstrations improves control generalization. Model architecture affects how effectively these experiences are used, while scaling pretraining under the selected configuration brings further gains. The resulting recipe, post-trained on RoboTwin Clean demonstrations only, achieves success rates of 88.10% and 61.56% under Easy (Clean-to-Clean) and Hard (Clean-to-Random) conditions, respectively. Our model achieves 40.00% SR across three real-world tasks, compared with 23.33% for the strongest baseline, indicating better generalization under unseen conditions. We release the curated data, training code, and model weights.

papers.title: SPARK: Simple Post-training for Adapting pRetrained Knowledge to Robot Control
papers.authors: Taekyung Kim, Jeongeun Park, Byeongho Heo, Sungjoon Choi, Sangdoo Yun, Dongyoon Han
papers.abstract: Large-scale representation learning has produced public foundation models that provide strong general-purpose visual features. However, their pretraining objectives are not designed for robot representation learning, so the resulting embeddings tend to emphasize global semantics rather than the temporally sensitive representations required for robot control. Training robot models from scratch is also undesirable due to the limited scale and high collection cost of robotics data, as well as the substantial computational burden of pre-training. In this paper, we propose SPARK (Simple Post-training for Adapting pRetrained Knowledge), a post-training method that adapts foundation models to robot control. SPARK is built on two principles: temporal abstraction, which encourages the encoder to derive compact features that preserve information essential for understanding temporal changes and action-relevant scene structure, and knowledge preservation, which aligns patch-level representations with those of the original foundation model to retain useful pretrained semantics. These objectives yield compact visual state representations that remain semantically meaningful while preserving useful prior knowledge. Experiments across multiple robotics benchmarks show that SPARK consistently improves success rates and generalization over vanilla foundation models, and further demonstrate that these gains transfer to real-world robot manipulation.

papers.title: SAM-VTP: Video Memory and Measured Geometry for Continuous Traversability Segmentation
papers.authors: Lucas Hoefs, Hui Xie, Senjian An, Fangyi Zhang
papers.abstract: Traversability prediction is a core component of autonomous navigation, yet most vision-based methods operate frame-wise and produce temporally inconsistent predictions. We present SAM-VTP (Video Traversability Prediction), which fine-tunes SAM2's video memory pathway for dense, prompt-free traversability segmentation, conditioning each frame on a persistent memory of prior observations. Rather than inferring terrain geometry from appearance, we measure it: slope, roughness and height are computed from depth and fused into the image features. We also introduce an offline continuous supervision pipeline that generates dense per-pixel traversability targets in [0,1] from depth-derived geometry and semantic priors, requiring no robot deployment and no per-pixel annotation, capturing conditional feasibility that binary labels cannot represent. On TartanGround, a large-scale synthetic ground-robot dataset, SAM-VTP improves fuzzy Jaccard from 0.908 to 0.924 and binary IoU from 0.854 to 0.886 over SAM-TP, a frame-wise SAM2 baseline, against a seed-to-seed spread below 0.001, and cuts frame-to-frame flicker by 31%. In closed-loop trials at two field sites, driving the same planner and controller, the baseline's dropouts leave the planner without a feasible path 3.3x more often on a paved course and 6.9x on rough ground, while SAM-VTP runs at 21.4 FPS on the Orin Nano the robot carries.

papers.title: RoboACE: Adversarial Co-Evolution for Robot Self-Improvement
papers.authors: Delin Zhao, Zhengrong Yue, Junlin He, Yali Wang
papers.abstract: Robot agents can improve reusable skills, planning procedures, and recovery strategies from execution feedback, yet a fixed practice source leaves the search for new weaknesses unchanged. Useful practice depends on the agent's current capabilities, so the procedure that chooses practice must also be revisable. We present RoboACE (Robot Adversarial Co-Evolution), a framework that jointly evolves curriculum and execution harnesses around frozen foundation models. The curriculum harness uses accumulated capability evidence to propose informative challenges, while the execution harness responds with reusable revisions that expand execution capabilities. Alternating updates hold one side fixed as the other changes, and admitted challenges form fixed snapshots for comparing execution revisions. Starting from a compact set of LIBERO practice conditions, the resulting frozen deployment outperforms the evaluated controllers and agent systems across four LIBERO-family panels. On LIBERO-PRO, it reaches 74.0% success, exceeding the initial deployment by 15.0 percentage points and direct execution by its VLA controller by 13.5 points. Case studies document changes to evidence-guided practice selection, drawer-skill grounding, and controller intervention.

papers.title: Robo-MLT: Dual-System Robotic Manipulation for Long-Horizon Medical Laboratory Tasks
papers.authors: Zequan Zeng, Kai Wang, Delvin Ce Zhang, Huaping Liu, Zhipeng Yuan, Junqin Yang, YunLong Zhang
papers.abstract: Reliable medical laboratory automation requires robots to complete entire workflows in protocol order while handling changes during execution. A robot may execute each motion correctly yet fail the workflow by confusing visually similar stages or stalling after human intervention. We present Robo-MLT, a dual-system framework that couples explicit workflow monitoring with learned action generation. A vision--language planner composes an ordered atomic-skill sequence from the protocol and the initial workspace observation. A multiframe execution monitor detects when the active skill has completed or become infeasible, then advances the workflow or triggers replanning. A skill-conditioned vision--language--action policy generates the manipulation trajectories, and an asynchronous runtime coordinates it with the monitor. We evaluate Robo-MLT against four policy baselines and a VLM-based monitor baseline on blood gas analysis and blood sample tube sorting, with 50 nominal configurations per method and 20 sample-removal configurations. Robo-MLT achieves task success rates of 82\% and 70\%, exceeding $π_{0.5}$ by 30 and 22 percentage points, respectively. After an operator removes the sample being handled, the system revises the remaining plan and continues processing the other samples. These results indicate that, under the evaluated conditions, explicit workflow monitoring makes long-horizon laboratory manipulation more reliable and recoverable.
